Agent Boundary Map
Agent Boundary Map

See where your agent puts its trust

For teams that build or configure AI agents—whether in your own code or on a harness such as Claude Code or Codex. Map each trust boundary: what enforces it, and whether that enforcement is independent of the model’s instructions and decisions.

The questions changed, so answers saved from the earlier version were cleared.

  • Nothing to upload. You describe your setup by answering questions: no code, configuration or logs.
  • Your answers stay in this browser. The page makes no network requests, and its security policy blocks them.
  • Why each question is here: the evidence ↗, from real incidents, research and security standards.
How it works
  1. Describe your agent. What runs it, and which parts it has: tools, memory, MCP servers and more. You only get questions about those parts.
  2. Answer how each boundary holds. Answer for the least-protected route. If you cannot verify a control, choose “Don’t know”: the report will show what to investigate.
  3. Get your report. It opens with the routes untrusted input could take: could one injected message make the agent read sensitive information and send it out, or change things? Then each finding, with what to do. Save it as a PDF or Markdown, in summary or in full.

Example map: a repo maintenance agent configured on Codex.

Each box takes the color of its weakest answer and gets darker as more of its answers are unprotected. The count shows how many answers are unprotected (not protected, or relying only on the model); the bar shows every scored answer in that step.

The rule behind every question: the model may propose, but something outside the model must authorize.
